title: Sunset from indoors
hook: a window, a lamp and a pause are enough

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nathanael, the skeptic Philip didn't argue with, and a sunset shared. Your line was come and see.

It's raining. It's winter, and the sun sets while you're still at work. Your window faces a brick wall. You're caring for someone and can't step out. A sunset ritual is lovely when the sky cooperates, but real life doesn't always. Does the ritual just stop? It doesn't have to. People have been marking dusk indoors for as long as there have been indoors.
screen: `RAIN, WORK, A BRICK WALL.` → `DOES THE RITUAL STOP?` → `SUNSET FROM INDOORS.`

segments.voice: For most of history, sunset meant one practical thing: light a lamp. Many traditions turned that ordinary moment into something more, each for its own reasons. Early Christians gathered at dusk for the lighting of the lamps and sang a Greek hymn called Phos Hilaron, often translated O gladsome light, or O joyful light. It's one of the oldest Christian hymns that survive outside the Bible; in the three hundreds, Basil the Great already called it ancient. Orthodox Christians still sing it at vespers as the evening light fades. In many Hindu homes, someone lights an oil lamp, a diya, at dusk, often before an image of God, and the evening prayers begin. And as you saw this week, Jewish homes light candles as Shabbat arrives on Friday. Different meanings, different words, different understandings of what the light is. But the gesture is the one your great-great-grandparents made every evening without thinking: the sky goes dark, so you strike a light. That's all today's practice needs. A window, even a small one, to notice the light changing. A lamp, turned on by hand when you notice. And a pause, a few breaths long, between the day and the evening. You don't need a horizon. You need to mark the turn. Without a marker, days blur into one long screen-lit stretch. With one, even a tiny one, the day has an ending, and an ending is what lets the evening begin.
screen: `SUNSET MEANT: LIGHT A LAMP.` · `PHOS HILARON, O GLADSOME LIGHT.` · `A DIYA AT DUSK.` · `A WINDOW, A LAMP, A PAUSE.` · then, large: `THE DAY TURNS.`

segments.voice: Picture the lamp you'll use tonight, a table lamp, a candle if it's safe, the light over the stove, and the window nearest it. When the light outside fades, you'll switch it on by hand, slowly, on purpose, then stand for three breaths. Rehearse it now: reach, switch, breathe.
Phos Hilaron, the ancient Greek hymn early Christians sang at dusk as the lamps were lit. Today's word.
Your line: the day turns. Next week, you build your own routine. Day one hundred fifty-two, done.
